title: Montaigne and the Return of Doubt
subtitle: A nobleman in a tower invents the essay and asks: what do I know?
objectives: By the end you will be able to describe Montaigne's life and why he invented the essay as a form of philosophy.
Explain his motto “What do I know?” and how it revived ancient skepticism.
Summarize the argument of “Of Cannibals” and evaluate it as an early form of cultural relativism.
Discuss Montaigne's method of self-examination and its influence on later thinkers.
Compare Montaigne's doubt with the skeptics of Day 27 and with Descartes' doubt on Day 43.
hook:
On his thirty-eighth birthday, in 1571, a French magistrate named Michel de Montaigne retired from public life. He had an inscription painted in Latin on the wall of a small room next to his library, announcing that, long weary of the servitude of the courts and public duties, he was withdrawing into the bosom of the learned Muses, where he hoped to spend what little remained of his life in calm and freedom.

His retreat was a round tower on his family estate near Bordeaux. On the ceiling beams of his library he had sayings painted, many of them from ancient skeptics and from the Bible, such as the remark from Ecclesiastes that God has given man a longing for knowledge in order to torment him. Outside, France was tearing itself apart in the Wars of Religion between Catholics and Protestants. Inside, Montaigne began writing short pieces about anything at all: sadness, idleness, liars, thumbs, smells, cannibals, the education of children, how to face death, his kidney stones, his cat.

He called these pieces *essais*, “attempts” or “trials.” He was not trying to build a system or prove a doctrine. He was testing himself, trying out his judgment on whatever came along. In doing so he invented a new literary form and a new way of doing philosophy, one in which the philosopher's own wavering, contradictory self is the main subject. Today we explore that form and the doubt at its heart.

sections.heading: A Life Between the Tower and the World
sections.body:
**Michel de Montaigne** (1533–1592) was born into a recently ennobled family of merchants near Bordeaux. His father had unusual ideas about education. Montaigne tells us that as an infant he was sent to live with a poor peasant family so that he would bond with ordinary people, and that afterward his father arranged for him to learn Latin as his first language: tutors and even servants were instructed to speak to the boy only in Latin. He was also woken each morning by music, so as not to jolt his tender brain. We have these stories from Montaigne himself, so they may be partly polished, but they help explain his lifelong ease with classical authors.

He studied law and served for thirteen years as a counselor in the Parlement of Bordeaux, a regional high court. There he met the great friendship of his life, the writer and magistrate Étienne de La Boétie. When La Boétie died in 1563, Montaigne was devastated. Years later, in his essay on friendship, he tried to explain why they had loved each other, and could say only: because it was he, because it was I.

Retirement in 1571 did not mean withdrawal from the world for good. Montaigne traveled through Germany, Switzerland and Italy in 1580–81, partly in search of cures for kidney stones, and while abroad learned he had been elected mayor of Bordeaux, a post he held for two terms (1581–85). He acted as a go-between for the Catholic king and the Protestant Henry of Navarre, the future Henry IV. During one of the plague outbreaks he and his family had to wander as refugees.

The *Essays* appeared in two books in 1580, an expanded edition with a third book in 1588, and a final posthumous edition in 1595 prepared by his devoted younger friend Marie de Gournay, herself a writer who argued for the equality of men and women. Montaigne kept adding to his essays rather than correcting them, so that his later thoughts sit beside his earlier ones, sometimes contradicting them. That, he thought, was honest: he was painting a self that was always changing.

sections.heading: The Essay: Philosophy as Trying Out
sections.body:
The word **essay** comes from the French *essai*, meaning an attempt, test or trial, the way you might assay a metal to see what it is made of. Montaigne's essays are not tidy arguments with introduction, thesis and conclusion like the school essays you may have written. They wander. An essay titled “Of Coaches” spends most of its time on the Spanish conquest of the Americas. One titled “Of Experience” moves from the impossibility of perfect laws to his diet, sleep and bowel habits, and to how to live well.

This wandering is a philosophical choice. Montaigne thought that human judgment is shifting and partial, and that the honest way to write is to follow the movement of a mind thinking. In his note “To the Reader,” he says that he himself is the matter of his book, and that he wants to be seen in his simple, natural, ordinary fashion, without straining or artifice.

This was startling. Augustine's *Confessions* (Day 30) had looked inward too, but Augustine was telling the story of a soul's journey to God. Montaigne studies himself because he is a specimen of humanity: each person, he said, bears the entire form of the human condition. By examining one ordinary person closely, with all his inconsistencies, we learn about everyone.

The method is **self-examination**, but not the kind that ends in a confident verdict. Montaigne finds himself inconsistent, changeable, sometimes bold and sometimes timid, sometimes generous and sometimes stingy. We are all patchwork, he says, so shapeless and diverse in composition that each bit, each moment, plays its own game. The Socratic command to know yourself (Day 9) turns out to be an endless task, because the self keeps moving. Remember Heraclitus and his river (Day 4)? Montaigne applies the same insight to the self.

sections.heading: “Que sais-je?”: The Revival of Skepticism
sections.body:
In 1576 Montaigne had a medal struck bearing an image of a set of scales in balance and his motto: ***Que sais-je?*** “What do I know?” The balanced scales echo the ancient skeptics' technique of setting arguments of equal weight against each other until the mind suspends judgment.

Remember Day 27? Pyrrho, Sextus Empiricus and the ancient skeptics practiced **epochē**, suspension of judgment, and found that it brought **ataraxia**, tranquility. Sextus' *Outlines of Pyrrhonism* had been printed in a Latin translation in 1562, and it hit the educated European world with real force. Montaigne absorbed it deeply. Several of the sayings on his library beams come from Sextus.

Montaigne's longest essay, the “Apology for Raymond Sebond,” is his great skeptical work. His father had asked him to translate a fifteenth-century book of natural theology by Raymond Sebond, which claimed to prove the Christian faith by reason. In the “Apology,” supposedly defending Sebond, Montaigne launches an extraordinary attack on human pretensions to knowledge:

- **Human beings are not superior to animals in the ways we assume.** Animals communicate, plan, show skill and loyalty. He writes, in a famous line: when I play with my cat, who knows if I am not a pastime to her more than she is to me?
- **The senses deceive.** Things look different depending on illness, distance, mood or the medium they pass through.
- **Reason contradicts itself.** Philosophers have disagreed endlessly about everything, which suggests that reason cannot settle the deepest questions.
- **Custom shapes belief.** What seems obvious in one country is absurd in another.

What follows from all this? For Montaigne, not despair but humility. Since reason cannot reach certainty about ultimate things, we should hold our opinions loosely, avoid cruelty and persecution in their name, and, in matters of religion, rely on faith and the customs of our country. This position, using skeptical doubt to undermine the pretensions of reason and leaving room for faith, is called **fideism**. Some readers, then and now, have suspected Montaigne's professed Catholic piety of masking a deeper unbelief. Most scholars take his Catholicism as sincere, though his religion is notably quiet, undogmatic and practical. Either way, in a country where people were killing each other over theology, his conclusion was pointed. As he later wrote about the witch trials of his day, it is putting a very high price on one's conjectures to have a man roasted alive because of them.

sections.heading: “Of Cannibals”: Who Are the Barbarians?
sections.body:
Montaigne's most famous essay, “Of Cannibals” (c. 1580), is about the Tupinambá people of the coast of Brazil, whom French travelers had encountered. Montaigne drew on reports from a servant who had lived there and from travel writers, and he says he spoke, through a poor interpreter, with three Tupinambá men brought to Rouen in the presence of the young King Charles IX.

The Tupinambá practiced ritual cannibalism: they killed and ate prisoners of war. Europeans called them savages. Montaigne's response is one of the most famous reversals in the history of thought. He argues that there is nothing barbarous or savage in that nation, except that each man calls barbarism whatever is not his own practice. We have no other test of truth and reason, he says, than the example and pattern of the opinions and customs of the country we live in.

He then turns the mirror on Europe. The Tupinambá eat their dead enemies; but Europeans tear living bodies apart by torture, roast people by degrees, and have dogs and pigs gnaw them, and they do it, he notes, not among ancient enemies but among neighbors and fellow citizens, under the pretext of piety and religion. He thinks there is more barbarity in eating a man alive than in eating him dead.

The essay ends with the three Tupinambá visitors' reactions to France. Asked what they found most remarkable, they said they were amazed that tall, bearded, armed men would obey a child king, and that some people were gorged with every good thing while their “halves,” their fellow human beings, begged at their doors starving, yet the poor did not seize the rich by the throat or set fire to their houses. Then Montaigne adds his famous ironic close: all this is not too bad, but what's the use? They don't wear breeches.

This is an early and powerful expression of **cultural relativism**: the idea that judgments of what is normal, civilized or right are shaped by the culture doing the judging. It is also a use of the outsider's eye to make one's own society strange, the technique we saw in More's *Utopia* (Day 38).

sections.heading: Is Montaigne a Relativist? Strengths and Limits
sections.body:
It is tempting to read “Of Cannibals” as saying that all cultures are equally good and no one can judge another. But look closely, and Montaigne is doing something more interesting.

First, he *does* judge. He calls the Tupinambá practice of eating enemies barbarous by the standard of reason, while insisting that European torture is worse. He measures both cultures against a standard, nature and reason, that he thinks they can both fail. So his relativism is better described as a critique of **ethnocentrism**, the habit of using one's own culture as the measure of all others, than as a denial of all moral standards.

Second, he idealizes the Tupinambá in ways that reveal his own agenda. He describes them as living close to nature, without commerce, letters, magistrates, rich and poor, or words for lying and treachery. This picture owes as much to classical myths of a Golden Age and to his wish to criticize France as to actual knowledge of Brazilian society. This is an early version of the **noble savage** trope, which would flourish in the eighteenth century and which anthropologists now criticize for flattening real people into symbols.

Third, there is a tension between skepticism and moral outrage. If custom shapes all our judgments, where does Montaigne stand when he condemns the cruelty of the Wars of Religion, or the Spanish conquest in “Of Coaches”? One answer is that Montaigne's skepticism targets grand theoretical claims, about God, nature and metaphysics, while leaving untouched the plain human revulsion at cruelty. He called cruelty the extreme of all vices. The philosopher Judith Shklar later built a whole political theory, the “liberalism of fear,” on the Montaignean idea of putting cruelty first.

This kind of modest, practical, anti-dogmatic stance is sometimes called **mitigated skepticism**: doubt about the big theories combined with trust in ordinary life, custom and decency. It looks forward to David Hume (Day 49).

sections.heading: Montaigne's Legacy: From Pascal to Descartes
sections.body:
Montaigne's influence was enormous and immediate. Shakespeare drew on John Florio's 1603 English translation of the *Essays*; a speech in *The Tempest* about an ideal commonwealth closely follows a passage in “Of Cannibals.” Francis Bacon (Day 41) borrowed the title *Essays* for his own collection. Blaise Pascal read Montaigne obsessively and was both fascinated and horrified by his calm acceptance of uncertainty.

Most importantly for our story, Montaigne helped create the intellectual crisis that the next generation tried to solve. The historian of philosophy Richard Popkin argued that the revival of ancient skepticism in the sixteenth century, through Sextus, Montaigne and his follower Pierre Charron, produced a “skeptical crisis.” If the senses deceive, reason contradicts itself and custom shapes belief, how can anything be known for certain? And in an age of religious conflict, if neither Catholics nor Protestants could prove their rule of faith, what then?

Reactions diverged. Some, like Montaigne, settled into a calm, humble skepticism. Others, like Pascal, concluded that only faith could rescue humanity from uncertainty. And one young Frenchman, educated at a Jesuit college where he read the ancients and the moderns, decided to take skeptical doubt further than anyone had, to doubt *everything* that could be doubted, precisely in order to find something that could not. His name was René Descartes, and on Day 43 we will see how he used Montaigne's weapon against Montaigne's conclusion.

The difference is revealing. For Montaigne, doubt is a way of life, a permanent companion that makes us humble, tolerant and attentive to experience. For Descartes, doubt is a tool, a temporary method for clearing the ground before building a system of certain knowledge. Which attitude is wiser remains a live question.

keyQuote.source: Montaigne's personal motto, struck on a medal in 1576 and discussed in the Essays, “Apology for Raymond Sebond”

modernConnection.title: Blogs, Bias and the Anthropologist's Eye
modernConnection.body:
Montaigne is often called the patron saint of bloggers, and for good reason. The personal essay, the newsletter, the reflective podcast and the long social media thread all descend from his idea that one ordinary person, honestly describing their own experience, quirks and changing opinions, can say something about everyone. The writer Sarah Bakewell, whose biography of Montaigne became a bestseller, argued that he would have felt at home in a world of self-revealing online writing.

But the comparison is double-edged. Montaigne's self-portrait was meant to be honest about weakness and inconsistency, while much online self-presentation is curated to look impressive. And his doubt is the opposite of the confident hot take. He would be suspicious of anyone who could produce a firm opinion on every topic every day. The question “What do I know?” would make a fine motto for anyone about to share a viral claim.

Montaigne's ideas also live on in modern psychology. Research on cognitive biases, confirmation bias, overconfidence and the tendency to see one's own group as the norm, gives experimental support to his observations that judgment is shaped by mood, custom and self-interest. Psychologists Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan pointed out in 2010 that most psychology studies used participants from WEIRD societies (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich and Democratic), who often turned out to be unusual rather than typical of humanity. That is a scientific version of Montaigne's warning against measuring everyone by the customs of one's own country.

Finally, “Of Cannibals” prefigures the methods of modern **cultural anthropology**, which asks researchers to understand practices from the inside before judging them. Yet the essay's limits are instructive too. Montaigne never visited Brazil and relied on secondhand reports, and his idealized portrait served his own critique of France. Modern anthropologists worry about exactly that: using other peoples as mirrors for our own concerns. And the debate over relativism continues. Can we condemn practices like torture or forced marriage across cultures? Montaigne's answer, condemn cruelty everywhere, including at home, but be slow to call unfamiliar customs barbaric, remains a useful starting point.

vocabulary.definition: From the French essai, an attempt or trial: Montaigne's new literary form, a short, exploratory, personal piece that tests the writer's judgment on a subject.
vocabulary.example: Montaigne's essay on experience wanders from law to his own diet and sleep.

vocabulary.definition: French for “What do I know?”: Montaigne's skeptical motto, symbolizing suspended judgment and intellectual humility.
vocabulary.example: Asking “Que sais-je?” before arguing about a hotly disputed issue is a good habit.

vocabulary.definition: The view that religious belief rests on faith rather than reason, often combined with skepticism about reason's ability to reach religious truth.
vocabulary.example: Montaigne's fideism used doubt about reason to leave room for faith and custom.

vocabulary.definition: The idea that beliefs about what is normal, civilized or right are shaped by one's culture, so that judging other cultures by one's own standards is suspect.
vocabulary.example: “Of Cannibals” is an early and influential expression of cultural relativism.

vocabulary.definition: The habit of judging other cultures by the standards of one's own, treating one's own customs as the natural norm.
vocabulary.example: Calling every unfamiliar food “disgusting” is a small case of ethnocentrism.

vocabulary.definition: The idealized image of non-European peoples as innocent, natural and uncorrupted by civilization; now criticized as a stereotype.
vocabulary.example: Montaigne's picture of the Tupinambá drifts toward the noble savage stereotype.

vocabulary.definition: A moderate doubt that rejects certainty about grand theoretical questions while trusting ordinary experience, custom and common decency for practical life.
vocabulary.example: Montaigne's mitigated skepticism left him doubtful about metaphysics but sure that cruelty is wrong.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of closely observing and reflecting on one's own thoughts, feelings and behavior to understand oneself and the human condition.
vocabulary.example: Montaigne's self-examination revealed that he was inconsistent from one moment to the next.

thinkingExercise.title: Write a Montaigne-Style Essay
thinkingExercise.prompt: Write a short essai of 300 to 500 words in Montaigne's spirit. Choose a small, ordinary subject (for example sleep, phones, anger, a habit you have, a food, a pet, waiting in line). The goal is not to prove a thesis but to try out your judgment and notice how your mind moves.
steps: Begin with a concrete observation from your own experience of the subject, as specific and honest as you can make it.
Bring in at least one other perspective: how someone from another culture, another era or another age group might see the same thing differently.
Notice and write down at least one inconsistency in yourself regarding the subject (you believe one thing but do another, or you feel differently on different days).
End not with a conclusion but with a question in the spirit of “What do I know?” Then reflect for a few minutes: did writing this way change what you think, compared to arguing for a fixed position?

summary: Montaigne, a French magistrate and later mayor of Bordeaux, retired to his tower in 1571 and invented the essay, an exploratory form of writing in which the self is the subject.
His motto “Que sais-je?” and his “Apology for Raymond Sebond” revived ancient Pyrrhonian skepticism, attacking human pretensions to certain knowledge and leading to humility and fideism.
“Of Cannibals” argues that each culture calls barbarism whatever is not its own custom, and that European torture is worse than Tupinambá cannibalism.
Montaigne's relativism is best read as a critique of ethnocentrism and cruelty rather than a denial of all standards, though his portrait of the Tupinambá is idealized.
His skepticism helped create a crisis of certainty that Descartes would try to answer by turning doubt into a method.

quiz.question: What does the French word essai, which Montaigne used for his writings, mean?
options: A proof
An attempt or trial
A sermon
A letter
quiz.explanation: An essai is an attempt or test; Montaigne was trying out his judgment rather than proving fixed doctrines.

quiz.question: Montaigne's motto “Que sais-je?” and its emblem of balanced scales reflect the influence of:
options: Aristotle's syllogistic logic
Plato's theory of Forms
Machiavelli's political realism
Ancient Pyrrhonian skepticism, especially Sextus Empiricus
quiz.explanation: Balanced scales evoke the skeptics' method of opposing equally weighty arguments until judgment is suspended; Sextus had recently been printed in Latin.

quiz.question: What was Montaigne's main purpose in writing about himself?
options: To show that he was a model of virtue
To tell the story of his conversion to God
To study one ordinary human being as a specimen of the human condition
To argue that he was smarter than other philosophers
quiz.explanation: Montaigne believed each person bears the entire form of the human condition, so honest self-study reveals something about everyone.

quiz.question: In the “Apology for Raymond Sebond,” Montaigne argues that human reason is reliable enough to settle all disputes about God and nature.
quiz.explanation: The Apology is a skeptical attack on reason's pretensions; Montaigne concludes we should be humble and rely on faith in religious matters.

quiz.question: What is Montaigne's central claim in “Of Cannibals”?
options: Each person calls barbarism whatever is not their own custom, and Europeans commit worse cruelties than the cannibals
The Tupinambá should be converted and civilized as soon as possible
Cannibalism is morally acceptable in all circumstances
Europeans are superior because they have writing and commerce
quiz.explanation: Montaigne reverses the usual judgment, arguing that torturing the living, as Europeans did, is more barbarous than eating the dead.

quiz.question: Why is Montaigne's view in “Of Cannibals” better described as a critique of ethnocentrism than as total relativism?
options: Because he says European customs are always best
Because he never judges any practice at all
Because he refuses to discuss morality
Because he still judges both cultures by a standard of reason and nature, condemning cruelty wherever it occurs
quiz.explanation: He calls cannibalism barbarous by reason's standard while insisting European torture is worse, so he does not abandon all standards.

quiz.question: Montaigne's portrait of the Tupinambá has been criticized for idealizing them as “noble savages” to serve his critique of France.
quiz.explanation: He relied on secondhand reports and described them as uncorrupted by civilization, an image that served his own purposes.

quiz.question: A researcher realizes that her psychology findings, based only on American college students, may not apply to people in other societies. Which Montaignean idea does this best illustrate?
options: Fideism
The divine right of kings
Warning against measuring all humanity by the customs of one's own country
The doctrine of double effect
quiz.explanation: Montaigne warned that we take our own customs as the measure of truth and reason; modern critiques of WEIRD samples make a similar point.

quiz.question: How does Montaigne's attitude to doubt differ from Descartes' (Day 43)?
options: Montaigne never doubted anything
For Montaigne doubt is a lasting way of life leading to humility; for Descartes it is a temporary method for reaching certainty
Descartes was more skeptical about God than Montaigne
They held exactly the same view
quiz.explanation: Montaigne lives with doubt; Descartes uses it as a tool to clear the ground for a certain foundation.

quiz.question: Montaigne's Essays were revised over many years, with later additions sitting alongside earlier passages rather than replacing them.
quiz.explanation: Montaigne preferred to add rather than correct, so that the book records a changing self; the posthumous 1595 edition was prepared by Marie de Gournay.

goDeeper.body:
Richard Popkin's *The History of Scepticism* (first published 1960, later expanded) is one of the most influential works in the history of early modern philosophy. Popkin argued that the Reformation created a “problem of the criterion”: Luther claimed that conscience reading scripture was the rule of faith, Catholics claimed it was the Church, and neither side could prove its criterion without circular reasoning. At the very same time, the rediscovery of Sextus Empiricus supplied ancient tools for exploiting exactly this kind of circle. Montaigne, on this account, became the central figure of a “nouveau Pyrrhonisme,” and much of seventeenth-century philosophy, Descartes above all, can be read as a series of responses to the skeptical crisis.

Critics have questioned whether the crisis was as widespread or as central as Popkin claimed, and whether Montaigne is really a Pyrrhonist at all. Some scholars stress the influence of Academic skepticism (Cicero) and Stoicism on Montaigne, and his intellectual development over time: early essays are more Stoic, preparing for death; the “Apology” is more skeptical; and the late essays, especially “Of Experience,” arrive at an earthy, joyful acceptance of bodily life. He concludes that the most beautiful lives are those that conform to the common human pattern, with order but without miracle and without extravagance.

Another debate concerns Montaigne's place in political thought. Shklar's “liberalism of fear” and other readings place him as a forerunner of toleration and liberalism, while others see him as a conservative who counseled obedience to the established order precisely because reason could not justify anything better. Both readings can find support in the text, which is perhaps the most Montaignean outcome possible.

readings.title: The Complete Essays
readings.author: Michel de Montaigne (trans. M. A. Screech or Donald Frame)
readings.note: Start with “Of Cannibals,” “Of Friendship,” “Of the Inconsistency of Our Actions” and “Of Experience.”

readings.title: How to Live: Or A Life of Montaigne in One Question and Twenty Attempts at an Answer
readings.author: Sarah Bakewell
readings.note: An engaging, accurate biography organized around Montaigne's practical wisdom.

readings.title: The History of Scepticism: From Savonarola to Bayle
readings.author: Richard H. Popkin
readings.note: The classic scholarly account of the skeptical crisis Montaigne helped provoke.

readings.title: Ordinary Vices
readings.author: Judith N. Shklar
readings.note: Develops the Montaignean idea of putting cruelty first among the vices.

questions: Is it possible to criticize another culture's practices without falling into ethnocentrism? What would a fair standard look like?
Montaigne thought each person bears the whole human condition. Is studying yourself a good way to learn about humanity, or a dangerous one?
Is doubt better used as a permanent attitude (Montaigne) or as a temporary method (Descartes)?
